chapter: Early career, theaters and Cobb's Tea Room
title: First trumpet, hearing Brunies in Biloxi, and the Alamo theater pit under Tasso
summary: His father gave him a trumpet at ten; he recalls hearing Abbie and Merritt Brunies, playing the symphony, and his muted trumpet feature in the Alamo pit, praised in the press.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone

blocks.x: Never forget music. I love music. My father gave me a trumpet when I was 10 years of age. He went off and came back that afternoon and I played America for him. On the trumpet. I don't know, I must have had a natural ambiture. Because right now I can just get about eight notes out of my horn and I can't practice here. And I'm not going to run to the shrine just because anyone. I have other things to do, things that I would like to do. But I would love to play my trumpet again. But if I couldn't play it the way I want to play it, I'm not going to play it. Because they want me to take the stick. I remember I went on vacation to Miami with my wife and my mother-in-law and his wife. They lived in Daytona. So our pastor was in Daytona and took them to freedom of Miami. And the wife and I, we went to Havana because they didn't want to go out there had been. So they stayed in Miami. Havana was a beautiful place there. And I came back. So coming back to New Orleans, we stopped in Biloxi and we went in Barachefs because they had Abbey Bruness in there. Have you heard of Abbey Bruness? I heard him there. Great, great jazz man. George Bruness' brother. Merrick Bruness played trombone. Loud trombone, but good, but good. And Henny, I called him Henny, his name was Henry. He played in the district, the red light district. He could play more with his feet than some people could play with their hands. He used to put his foot up in the slide. And I'm telling you, I loved it. I was brought up as a legit musician. I played in New Orleans Symphony on the fresh air, but for all egotistical reasons, just to prove that I could. You know musicians are egotists. They love to play it, but when I played in the Alfie Theater, success came to me from the Alfie Theater. And I mean suddenly, and money. Of course I was getting a good salary at the Alfie Theater. I was getting $86 a week. I was married and we got a loan fine and all that. You know, we didn't have to pay much money. And my brother was my biggest booster. And one day we were playing the weekly, and I don't know whether they were dying or had a funeral, but Tasso was playing some old tune that only Emil Tasso, who was our greatest vaudeville leader. You've heard of him. His son is still living. We play a tune like that, but the changes, they lay natural for me. So my brother says, get with it. I say, what do you mean? He says, put the mute in and let him have it. And Tasso didn't expect it. It almost hit him in the head when I put the mute in and I started to do it nice and quiet. And they had a beautiful set of strings. We had two first violins, a viola, a shell and a bass that were out of this world. I got those full chords, the flute and the clarinet, they didn't intrude. And the trombonist was my sidekick. He didn't play at all because he didn't want to cover me. The tune was called China We All Out To You. Did you ever hear that tune? Never. I have never heard it since. Well, when I stopped, when we stopped, the house came down in the darkness. And then so on, I had to have something ready, which made it a hard job, 52 weeks in a week. But I have some write-ups that repay me. I have a write-up that says, with the exception of my trumpet playing, there was nothing in the show. How do you like that? And I saved it and I can show it to you.
Did they put a spotlight on you?
